176.title: Harden not your hearts (Psalm 94 [95])
176.hook: the psalm that opens the Church's daily prayer: today if you shall hear his voice
176.tomorrow: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 102 [103])
176.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours begin each day with the Invitatory: 'Lord, open my lips' with a small sign of the cross on the lips, then an antiphon and usually Psalm 94 [95], before the first hour of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a guardian angel, and a psalm the devil quoted. Your line was under his wings. A new week, and the psalm that most often opens the day.

Every morning, in monasteries, convents, rectories and a lot of ordinary kitchens, the Church's daily prayer begins with the same words. Before any psalm or reading, someone traces a small cross on their lips and says: Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise. It's a line from the Miserere, the psalm from five days ago. Then, right away, comes a psalm, on most days the same one. It's the doorbell of the whole day's prayer.
screen: `A CROSS TRACED ON THE LIPS.` → `LORD, OPEN MY LIPS.` → `THE DOORBELL OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: That opening is called the Invitatory, from the Latin for invitation. Its usual psalm is Psalm 94 in the Douay, 95 in most Bibles, and it begins exactly like an invitation: "Come let us praise the Lord with joy: let us joyfully sing to God our saviour." Come. Let's go. It's plural; nobody's praying alone. It moves through God as maker of the deep places of the earth and the mountain peaks, the sea and the dry land. Then it slows down: "Come let us adore and fall down: and weep before the Lord that made us. For he is the Lord our God: and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand." Then, suddenly, the tone changes: "To day if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts." God himself speaks, and recalls the desert, when their ancestors, thirsty and angry, tested God at a place called Massah and Meribah, testing and quarreling, though they'd seen everything he'd done. They heard, and their hearts went hard. A warning tucked inside an invitation. The Letter to the Hebrews presses on that one word, today: encourage one another every day, as long as it's still called today. Every morning, the Church hears it fresh. Not yesterday. Not some better tomorrow. Today. And the question it asks is simple: if God spoke to you today, in a person, a moment, a line you read, would you be soft enough to notice?
screen: `INVITATORY: AN INVITATION.` · `COME, LET US PRAISE.` · `TO DAY IF YOU SHALL HEAR HIS VOICE.` · `NOT YESTERDAY, NOT TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: Before saying anything, to God or to yourself, just listen: the room, the traffic, your own breathing, the small voice in you that says the thing you've been avoiding. Don't answer it yet; just hear it. Then, if you pray, trace a small cross on your lips and say, Lord, open my lips; if you don't, notice what you heard when you stopped talking.
Invitatory. The invitation that opens the Church's daily prayer, with the psalm that says: today, if you hear his voice. Today's word.
Your line: today, if you hear. The invitation comes new every morning. Day one hundred seventy-six, done.

177.title: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 102 [103])
177.hook: he knows we are dust, and his mercy is from eternity
177.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 102 [103] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it often at Mass as a responsorial psalm of mercy, with the refrain drawn from its line that the Lord is kind and merciful.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Invitatory, the invitation that opens each day's prayer. Your line was today, if you hear. Today, a psalm that talks to itself.

Have you ever talked to yourself out loud? Come on. You can do this. Don't forget your keys. Most people do it, usually under their breath, in the car or the kitchen. It's how you get your own attention. The psalms do it too. Several times, the one praying stops talking to God and turns to their own soul, like giving yourself a nudge. One psalm's opening is nothing but that: a pep talk to the self, about gratitude.
screen: `COME ON. YOU CAN DO THIS.` → `TALKING TO YOUR OWN SOUL.` → `A PEP TALK FOR GRATITUDE.`

segments.voice: Psalm 102 in the Douay, 103 in most Bibles: "Bless the Lord, O my soul: and let all that is within me bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and never forget all he hath done for thee." The Hebrew word for soul here, nephesh, doesn't mean a ghostly inner part. It means your whole living self, even your throat, your breath. So: all of me, wake up and remember. Why the reminder? Because we forget good things fast. The psalm makes a list: he forgives, he heals, he redeems your life from destruction, he crowns you with mercy, he renews your youth like an eagle's. Then come the tenderest lines about God in the whole psalter. "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our iniquities from us." East and west never meet; walk forever and you'll never reach where your sins went. "As a father hath compassion on his children, so hath the Lord compassion on them that fear him: for he knoweth our frame. He remembereth that we are dust." Not to shame us, but to go easy on us. Then our shortness again, like the psalm of Moses: "Man's days are as grass." A wind passes over the flower and it's gone. "But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon them that fear him." The flower is short. The mercy isn't. At the end it turns outward, angels, heavenly hosts, all his works, bless the Lord, then comes home: bless the Lord, O my soul.

segments.voice: Talk to yourself a little, the way the psalm does, come on, soul, remember, and find three good things from the past few days: not big ones, a meal, a text from a friend, a moment of sun, a thing that didn't go wrong. Name each one slowly and stay with it for a few breaths. If you pray, thank God for each, bless the Lord, O my soul; if you don't, let each one land fully before moving on.
Nephesh. The Hebrew word for soul: not a ghostly inner part, but your whole living self, breath and all. Today's word.
Your line: forget not his benefits. All that is within me, awake. See you tomorrow.

178.title: All creation (Psalm 103 [104])
178.hook: springs, cedars, wild goats, the sea full of creatures
178.howItsDone: Catholics sing Psalm 103 [104] as the responsorial psalm at Pentecost, with its line about sending forth the Spirit to renew the face of the earth, and at the Easter Vigil after the creation reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nephesh: a psalm giving its own soul a pep talk. Your line was forget not his benefits. Today, the very next psalm.

Put on a nature documentary. Mountain goats balanced on an impossible cliff. A whale surfacing, enormous and unhurried. Lions at dusk. A spring bubbling out of a rock, and birds lining up to drink. The narrator's voice goes quiet with wonder. Long before cameras, someone made the same film in words: a psalm that walks through the whole created world, one creature at a time.
screen: `GOATS ON A CLIFF.` → `A WHALE SURFACING.` → `A DOCUMENTARY IN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Psalm 103 in the Douay, 104 in most Bibles, opens with the same line as the psalm before it: bless the Lord, O my soul. This time the reason isn't mercy. It's the world. God is clothed with light as with a garment, stretching out the sky like a tent. Then the tour. Springs run down between the hills, and wild asses come to drink. Birds nest by the water and sing among the branches. Grass for the cattle, and for people, three gifts: "wine may cheer the heart of man," oil to make the face shine, and bread to strengthen the heart. The cedars of Lebanon, planted by God, with sparrows nesting there and the heron's house in the highest of them. Then a line the Douay makes delightful: "The highest mountains are a refuge for the harts, the rock for the irchins." Irchins are hedgehogs. The Hebrew seems to mean a small rock animal, the hyrax, but the Latin chose hedgehogs, so the Douay gave God's rocks to the hedgehogs. The moon marks the seasons, lions roar for their prey at night, and people go out to work until evening. Then the sea, with creatures without number, ships sailing across it, and the great sea creature, in the Douay a sea dragon, made "to play therein." At the summit: "How great are thy works, O Lord? thou hast made all things in wisdom." Everything waits on God for food; when God takes away their breath, they die. And then the line the Church sings at Pentecost: "Thou shalt send forth thy spirit, and they shall be created: and thou shalt renew the face of the earth."
screen: `CLOTHED WITH LIGHT.` · `WINE, OIL AND BREAD.` · `THE ROCK FOR THE IRCHINS.` · `A SEA CREATURE MADE TO PLAY.`

segments.voice: Step outside if you can, or look out a window, and like the psalm, make a slow list: a tree, a bird, a cloud, a dog walking its person, weeds in a crack in the sidewalk. Name each one quietly, and give it a breath before the next. If you pray, end with the psalm's line, how great are thy works, O Lord; if you don't, let the list be its own kind of wonder.
All creation. The psalm's tour of the world, from springs and cedars to hedgehogs and the sea, all made in wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: how great are thy works. Even the hedgehogs got a rock. That's day one hundred seventy-eight.

179.title: The Sunday evening psalm (Psalm 109 [110])
179.hook: the psalm that opens Sunday Vespers, about a priest forever like Melchisedech
179.tomorrow: From the rising of the sun (Psalm 112 [113])
179.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours say Vespers (Evening Prayer) at the end of the day, and on every Sunday it opens with Psalm 109 [110]; in cathedrals and monasteries it is often sung, sometimes with incense.

segments.voice: Yesterday, all creation, from springs and cedars to hedgehogs on the rocks. Your line was how great are thy works. Today, an evening psalm.

Sunday, late afternoon, the light going gold. In a monastery, a bell rings, and the monks file into their stalls, facing each other across the choir. In a cathedral side chapel, a handful of people gather. In a city apartment, someone opens an app. All about to pray the Church's evening prayer at the same hour. And every Sunday, week after week, it begins with the same psalm, about a king and a very mysterious priest.
screen: `SUNDAY, THE LIGHT GOING GOLD.` → `A BELL, AND THE MONKS FILE IN.` → `THE SAME PSALM EVERY SUNDAY.`

segments.voice: The evening prayer is called Vespers, from the Latin vesper, evening, the same word for the evening star. With Lauds in the morning, it's one of the two great hinges of the Church's daily prayer. It gathers up the day and offers it back, often with incense rising and a candle lit. Sunday Vespers opens with Psalm 109 in the Douay, 110 in most Bibles: "The Lord said to my Lord: Sit thou at my right hand: Until I make thy enemies thy footstool." It's a royal psalm, a king being enthroned. Jesus puzzled his listeners with it. Matthew says he asked, "What think you of Christ? whose son is he?" David's, they said. Then how can David call him my Lord? "If David then call him Lord, how is he his son?" No one could answer him a word. The New Testament comes back to this psalm again and again, hearing in it the risen Christ seated at God's right hand. Then the strangest line: "The Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech." Melchisedech appears in Genesis for just a few verses: a king of Salem who comes out to meet Abraham, "bringing forth bread and wine, for he was the priest of the most high God," and blesses him. Genesis gives him no family tree. The Letter to the Hebrews makes much of that, calling him without beginning of days or end of life, and builds its picture of Christ's priesthood on him. Catholics still hear his name in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer, and this psalm can be sung when priests are ordained: a priest for ever.
screen: `VESPERS: THE EVENING PRAYER.` · `SIT THOU AT MY RIGHT HAND.` · `HOW IS HE HIS SON?` · `A PRIEST LIKE MELCHISEDECH.`

segments.voice: Picture the light fading at the end of today, and look back over the day: what it held, what it cost, what you'd hand back. If you pray, offer the day to God the way Vespers does, perhaps with a line from a psalm you've learned; if you don't, simply watch the light change in your mind, and let the day end.
Vespers. The Church's evening prayer, which on Sundays opens with the psalm of a king and a priest for ever. Today's word.
Your line: a priest for ever. A priest with no family tree. Day one hundred seventy-nine, done.

180.title: From the rising of the sun (Psalm 112 [113])
180.hook: God stoops down to lift the poor from the dust
180.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 112 [113] at Evening Prayer on some Sundays and on feasts, and hear it at Mass; in Latin it is known as Laudate pueri, and composers have set it for Vespers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vespers, and a priest for ever like Melchisedech. Your line was a priest for ever. Today, a psalm that runs from sunrise to sunset.

Right now, somewhere on earth, the sun is rising. Somewhere else it's setting. At every moment, someone is waking up and someone is going to bed. A short psalm turns that fact into praise that never stops, a relay around the planet. And then, halfway through, it looks down from the sky, all the way down to the garbage heap at the edge of town.
screen: `ALWAYS SOMEONE'S SUNRISE.` → `PRAISE THAT NEVER STOPS.` → `DOWN TO THE GARBAGE HEAP.`

segments.voice: Psalm 112 in the Douay, 113 in most Bibles. It opens: "Praise the Lord, ye children: praise ye the name of the Lord." Children follows the Latin, pueri, a word that can also mean servants, and the Hebrew does say servants: you who serve the Lord. Then the sun: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise." East to west, morning to night. Then it climbs as high as it can go: God is high above all nations, his glory above the heavens. Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high? And then the surprise. This God looks down on the low things in heaven and in earth, and the psalm keeps going down: "Raising up the needy from the earth, and lifting up the poor out of the dunghill: That he may place him with princes, with the princes of his people." The dunghill was probably the town refuse heap, often explained as the place where the poorest people slept and begged. The God above the heavens stoops all the way to the dump and seats someone from there at the royal table. One more: the barren woman is given a home, the joyful mother of children. Hannah sings nearly the same lines about the poor and the dunghill when her son is born, and Mary sings the same turning-over of the world in the Magnificat. This psalm begins the Hallel, the psalms of praise sung at Passover. Some readers think these were the hymn Jesus and his friends sang at the Last Supper before going out to the Mount of Olives.
screen: `YE CHILDREN, YE SERVANTS.` · `FROM SUNRISE TO SUNSET.` · `OUT OF THE DUNGHILL, TO PRINCES.` · `HANNAH, MARY, THE HALLEL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who's low right now: discouraged, overlooked, stuck on their own small dunghill. Think of one small thing that might lift them a little: a message, a call, a true compliment, a coffee, an invitation to sit at your table. If you pray, pray for them in the psalm's words, raising up the needy; if you don't, simply hold them in mind and choose your one small thing.
Laudate pueri. Latin for praise, O servants, the psalm's name at Vespers, praise running around the world all day, to the God who stoops to lift the poor. Today's word.

181.title: The shortest psalm (Psalm 116 [117])
181.hook: two verses: praise the Lord, all nations
181.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 116 [117] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and it is often sung in Latin as Laudate Dominum; some pray it through the day as a short prayer of praise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laudate pueri: the God who stoops to lift the poor out of the dust. Your line was he raises the needy. Today, something much shorter.

Some psalms go on for pages. And then there's this one. You could say it while the kettle boils, or while a traffic light changes. Two verses, under thirty words in the Douay: the shortest psalm in the Psalter. And in those few words it invites the whole planet. Not one people, not one city, not one church. Everyone.
screen: `SOME PSALMS RUN FOR PAGES.` → `THIS ONE: TWO VERSES.` → `AND IT INVITES EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here is the whole thing, in the Douay-Rheims: "O praise the Lord, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people. For his mercy is confirmed upon us: and the truth of the Lord remaineth for ever." That's the psalm. First, the shape. Verse one is the invitation, as wide as it can be: all nations, all peoples. Verse two gives the reason, in two old Hebrew words that run all through the Psalms. Mercy is chesed, the steady, loyal love that keeps a promise. Truth is emet, faithfulness, the thing you can lean your weight on. So the whole world is invited to praise because God's love holds, and God's faithfulness lasts. Second, where it sits. Like yesterday's psalm, it belongs to the Hallel, the psalms of praise sung at Passover and the great feasts, and it's still sung in Jewish worship today. Third, who picked it up. Saint Paul quotes it in his letter to the Romans, to say the good news was meant for the nations, not one people alone. The Church kept singing it in Latin, Laudate Dominum, omnes gentes. Mozart set it to music, and pilgrims at Taizé sing it over and over. A Catholic can pray it at Vespers, a Jewish family sings it at Passover, and both are singing the same two verses about everyone.
screen: `TWO VERSES: THE INVITE AND THE REASON.` · `MERCY AND TRUTH: LOVE THAT HOLDS.` · `SUNG AT PASSOVER, THEN AND NOW.` · `PAUL, MOZART, TAIZÉ: ALL NATIONS.` · then, large: `O PRAISE THE LORD, ALL YE NATIONS.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say the two verses slowly three times: once as they are, once picturing a country you've never visited, with people waking up there right now, and once picturing someone near you who is nothing like you. If you don't pray, just hold those three pictures in the quiet: here, far away, and next door.
Laudate Dominum. Latin for praise the Lord, the shortest psalm in the whole Psalter: two verses that invite all nations. Today's word.
Your line: all nations. The psalm had room for them before you ever met them. That's day one hundred eighty-one.

182.title: The alphabet psalm (Psalm 118 [119])
182.hook: 176 verses in 22 stanzas, one for each Hebrew letter, all about God's word
182.howItsDone: Catholics pray portions of Psalm 118 [119] in the Liturgy of the Hours, especially at the midday hours, usually one stanza at a time, and some read one stanza a day as lectio divina.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shortest psalm, Laudate Dominum: two verses for the whole world. Your line was all nations. Today, the longest.

Maybe you learned the alphabet with a song. A is for apple, B is for ball, all the way to Z. Children love it because it has an order: you always know where you are and how far is left. Now imagine someone doing that with a prayer. Every letter of their alphabet, in order, eight lines for each. Twenty-two letters. A hundred seventy-six verses. The longest psalm in the Bible, and the longest chapter too.
screen: `A IS FOR APPLE.` → `EIGHT LINES FOR EVERY LETTER.` → `THE LONGEST PSALM OF ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the shape. In Hebrew, this psalm is an acrostic: twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav. All eight lines of the first stanza begin with aleph, every line of the second with beth, and so on to the end. Open a Douay-Rheims and you'll still see the letters printed as little headings: ALEPH, BETH, GHIMEL. English can't keep the trick, but it keeps the signposts. Second, the subject. All hundred seventy-six verses are about one thing: God's word. The poet keeps finding new names for it: law, testimonies, ways, precepts, commandments, justifications, words. Nearly every verse has one. It opens: "Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord." Third, the feeling. You might expect a psalm about law to sound like a rulebook. It sounds like a love letter. Halfway through, the poet says: "O how have I loved thy law, O Lord! it is my meditation all the day." For the psalmist, God's law isn't a fence. It's a gift, the way God has shown himself. Why an alphabet? Nobody knows for certain. Some say it helped people memorize it. Some say it's a way of saying everything, from A to Z, the whole of life, belongs to this love. Jews pray it, and so do Catholics: for centuries monks and priests prayed pieces of it every day in the Divine Office, a stanza or two at a time.
